approaches.name: Lateral approach to the femoral shaft (periprosthetic)
aliases: lateral vastus-elevating approach to the femur
approaches.corridor: Lateral approach splitting the fascia lata and elevating vastus lateralis off the lateral intermuscular septum and linea aspera, ligating profunda perforators, to expose the femoral shaft

sources.title: Lateral approach to the femoral shaft (periprosthetic)

procedure_applications.condition: A periprosthetic femoral fracture with a stable prosthesis or a fracture distal to the prosthesis is plated laterally
A femoral shaft fracture is plated through a lateral approach

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral decubitus with the lateral thigh accessible along the needed length of femur.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark a line between the greater trochanter and the lateral femoral epicondyle over the length required for the fracture.

incision.text: Incise along that line and open the fascia lata with a scalpel and scissors parallel to the incision along its fibers.

superficial_interval.text: Separate vastus lateralis bluntly from the fascia lata with a Cobb elevator and retract it anteromedially.

deep_interval.text: Incise the investing fascia about 1 cm anterior to the intermuscular septum and detach vastus lateralis from the septum and linea aspera with a periosteal elevator, identifying and ligating the profunda perforating vessels as they pierce the septum from behind.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, vastus lateralis, the perforating vessels at the lateral intermuscular septum, and the lateral femoral shaft.

structures_at_risk.text: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris at the septum are the main structures at risk; the femoral vessels and sciatic nerve lie medially and posteromedially and are not exposed by this approach.

danger_zones.text: The lateral intermuscular septum is the danger zone for perforating-vessel bleeding; a retracted, unligated perforator can cause troublesome occult bleeding.

retraction_hazards.text: Ligate larger perforators and cauterize smaller ones before they retract into the posterior compartment.

exposure.text: Exposes the lateral femoral shaft for plating over the required length.

limitations.text: It does not expose the medial or posterior neurovascular structures and relies on control of the perforating vessels.

indications.text: Indicated for periprosthetic femoral fractures with a stable prosthesis, fractures distal to a prosthesis, and femoral shaft plating.

closure.text: Let vastus lateralis fall back over the femur and repair it to its anterior and lateral origin where possible, closing in layers over a subfascial drain.

complications.text: Complications include perforating-vessel hematoma, and rarely injury to medial neurovascular structures if the far cortex is breached.

questions.question: Which vessels must be controlled during the lateral femoral approach?
questions.answer: The perforating branches of the profunda femoris at the lateral intermuscular septum.

questions.question: In which direction is vastus lateralis retracted?
Why are the femoral vessels and sciatic nerve usually safe in this approach?
questions.answer: They lie medially and posteromedially and are not exposed by the lateral dissection.

approaches.name: ASIS osteotomy to extend anterior pelvic exposure
approaches.corridor: Digastric osteotomy of the anterior superior iliac spine with the sartorius and inguinal ligament attached, reflected medially to widen anterior pelvic and acetabular exposure while sparing the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve

procedure_applications.condition: Additional anterior pelvic exposure is needed during an anterior acetabular approach
Extended anterior exposure is required for a periprosthetic acetabular fracture or revision

positioning.text: Position supine as part of an anterior pelvic or ilioinguinal exposure.

surface_landmarks.text: Identify the anterior superior iliac spine and the attached inguinal ligament and sartorius.

incision.text: Through the anterior pelvic incision, expose the ASIS while protecting the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

superficial_interval.text: Perform a digastric osteotomy of the ASIS with an osteotome or sagittal saw, keeping the sartorius and external oblique attached.

deep_interval.text: Retract the osteotomized ASIS with the sartorius and external oblique medially to widen access to the deeper pelvis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue with the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, the ASIS fragment with inguinal ligament and sartorius, and the inner pelvis.

structures_at_risk.text: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve at the ASIS and, with the anterior retractor, the superior gluteal artery and nerve are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The region of the ASIS is the danger zone for the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, and deep anterior retractor placement endangers the superior gluteal artery and nerve.

retraction_hazards.text: Place the anterior retractor carefully to avoid the superior gluteal artery and nerve and protect the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve.

exposure.text: Widens the anterior pelvic and acetabular exposure by reflecting the ASIS and its attached structures.

limitations.text: It is an adjunct that adds exposure to an anterior approach and carries a risk of osteotomy nonunion if not securely fixed.

indications.text: Indicated to extend anterior exposure for ORIF of periprosthetic acetabular fractures or revision arthroplasty.

closure.text: Repair the osteotomy with a single lag screw of at least 3.5 mm to resist nonunion and failure, then close in layers.

complications.text: Complications include osteotomy nonunion or escape, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve injury, and superior gluteal neurovascular injury.

questions.question: What remains attached to the osteotomized ASIS fragment?
questions.answer: The sartorius and the external oblique (with the inguinal ligament).

questions.question: Which nerve is most at risk during an ASIS osteotomy?
How is the ASIS osteotomy fixed at closure?
questions.answer: With a single lag screw of at least 3.5 mm to resist nonunion.
